title.en: Compute the summed field, do not overlay two animations

summary: Evaluate the total field as the sum of contributions at each point, rather than layering separate visuals.
objective: Make combined-source scenes show genuine interference and cancellation.
applies_when: Two or more sources, charges or waves contribute to one field.
Interference, cancellation or a null region is part of the message.
Sources can be moved or their strengths changed.
example_prompts: Show the field of two charges and where it cancels.
Let me move the sources and watch the combined pattern.
negative_signals: Single-source fields, where no combination is needed.
Nonlinear media, where simple superposition does not apply.
not_for: Single-source fields, where no combination is needed.
Nonlinear media, where simple superposition does not apply.

principles: Superposition is a computation, not a compositing operation. The total electric field of several sources is the vector sum of the fields each source would produce alone, evaluated at the same point.
Blending two rendered images cannot produce cancellation, because visual layers add brightness where fields subtract, which is precisely backwards at a null.
The interesting structure lives in the sum: nulls, saddle points and the shape of the transition are what a viewer should discover, and they exist only in the computed field.
The magnitude falls with distance in a specific way for each source type, so the sum is sensitive to placement, which makes moving the sources a genuinely informative interaction.

The vector sum stated here is the electrostatic case. Wave superposition adds signed or complex amplitudes with their phases, so a scene that combines waves must sum amplitudes rather than magnitudes, and interference nulls come from phase, not from opposed direction vectors.
implementation: Evaluate each source contribution at each sample point and sum the vectors before any visual mapping.

Choose the visual encoding after the sum: arrows, streamlines and magnitude colouring all derive from the summed vector field. Equipotential surfaces are a different object: they require the scalar potential, summed from the same sources with a stated reference point, and are not level sets of the field magnitude.
Handle the singular neighbourhood of a point source explicitly, with a stated cutoff or masked region.
Let sources be moved and the field recomputed, and mark null regions where the summed magnitude falls below a stated threshold.
Keep the sample resolution visible, since a coarse grid can miss a narrow null entirely.
observable_checks: Test both classic configurations and check the sign of the reasoning. Two equal same-sign charges give a genuine field null at the midpoint, because their contributions point in opposite directions. Two equal and opposite charges do the reverse: at the midpoint both contributions point from the positive towards the negative charge and reinforce, while it is the potential, not the field, that vanishes on the perpendicular bisector.
Compare a computed sample against a hand computation for a simple configuration.
Move one source and confirm the whole pattern updates rather than one layer sliding.
Refine the sample grid near a null and confirm the null is a real feature rather than a sampling artefact.

creative_affordances: Encoding of the summed field is free: particles, ribbons, colour or displacement all work.
Artistic exaggeration of magnitude is acceptable when the mapping is stated.
known_limits: Authored computation guidance citing the superposition of point-charge fields; nonlinear media and time-retarded fields are outside it.
No runtime field computation has been verified for this record.

claims.statement: The total electric field of several source charges is the vector sum of the fields that each source charge produces independently at that point, and the field of a single point charge is directed radially with magnitude proportional to the charge divided by the square of the distance.
claims.scope: Electrostatic fields of stationary point charges in vacuum; it does not cover time-varying or nonlinear situations.
